The study identified potential biases due to deviations from intended exposures, incomplete outcome data (attrition bias), and unclear risks in the measurement of outcomes, selection of reported results, and other biases. Additionally, there were concerns about random sequence generation (selection bias), allocation concealment (selection bias), blinding of participants and personnel (performance bias), blinding of outcome assessment (detection bias), and selective reporting (reporting bias). 2. In the study by Dursun (2006), postmenopausal women over the age of 40 in Turkey were included. Participants were recruited from osteoporosis outpatient clinics at Kocaeli University and the Middle East Technical University. Women with active gastrointestinal or liver disease, renal failure, malignancy, rheumatoid arthritis, or other inflammatory rheumatic diseases, as well as those on medications affecting bone metabolism, were excluded. Bone mineral density (BMD) of the lumbar spine and femoral neck was measured, and participants were categorized based on breastfeeding duration. 3. The Fagerhaug (2013) study utilized data from the Nord-Trøndelag Health Study (HUNT) in Norway, targeting adults aged 20 and above. Exclusion criteria included non-response to questionnaires, current pregnancy, age restrictions, and pre-existing conditions like myocardial infarction or diabetes before the first birth. Participants provided reproductive history, including lactation duration, and cardiovascular mortality was assessed through registry linkage. 4. The Fall (2011) study pooled data from 10,912 participants aged 15–41 from five birth-cohort studies in lowand middle-income countries. Breastfeeding duration was categorized into nine levels, and outcomes such as diabetes, impaired fasting glucose, hypertension, and prehypertension were analyzed. Biases related to confounding, participant selection, and exposure classification were noted. 5. Feldblum (1992) recruited women aged 40–54 in North Carolina through advertisements. Inclusion criteria required at least one intact ovary and no physical impairments, while exclusions included pregnancy, recent smoking, and chronic diseases. Participants completed questionnaires on lactation, and bone density was measured. Breastfeeding durations were categorized into three groups. 6. Ferguson (1981) analyzed data from the Christchurch Child Development Study in New Zealand, focusing on infants born in 1977. Breastfeeding was classified into five categories based on duration. Information on the child’s health and family situation was collected through structured interviews. 7. Fonseca (2010) studied children aged 5–10 in Portugal, with 1,976 participants included after exclusions. Parents provided data on breastfeeding and asthma, which was defined as self-reported and physician-diagnosed. Anthropometric measurements were also taken. 8. Fredriksson (2007) conducted a prospective cohort study in Finland, analyzing asthma incidence in children aged 1–7 over six years. Breastfeeding duration was categorized into five groups, and asthma was defined as doctor-diagnosed at follow-up. 9. Gay (2015) used data from the Singapore Breast Cancer Screening Project, involving 28,234 women aged 50–64. Participants completed questionnaires on reproductive factors, breastfeeding, and oral contraceptive use. Breastfeeding duration was calculated as the sum of all individual durations. 10. Gigante (2001) studied 5,304 children born in Pelotas, Brazil, in 1993. Breastfeeding duration was recorded at six and twelve months, and anthropometric outcomes were measured five years post-delivery, including BMI, waist circumference, and body fat percentage. 11. Girard (2019) analyzed data from the Encuesta Longitudinal de la Primera Infancia cohort in Chile, focusing on children aged 7–24 months. Breastfeeding duration was categorized into four groups, and behavioral problems were assessed using the CBCL 1½–5 parent report. 12. Grummer-Strawn (2004) utilized data from the CDC Pediatric Nutrition Surveillance System, which aggregates growth and anemia data from low-income children attending public health clinics.
